candidate.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — dietary sodium modification for a client with heart failure
candidate.educational_objective: Apply practical sodium-reduction strategies by reading labels, choosing lower-sodium prepared foods, and replacing added salt with non-sodium flavorings.

options.A: I will compare Nutrition Facts labels, choose lower-sodium packaged foods, and use herbs, spices, citrus, or vinegar instead of adding salt for flavor.
options.B: I can rely on taste to identify high-sodium foods, so reading labels is unnecessary if a food does not taste salty.
options.C: Processed and restaurant foods contribute little sodium, so I should focus mainly on removing the saltshaker from the table.
options.D: I should increase table salt at meals because sodium restriction is not relevant to dietary management when heart failure is present.

candidate.rationale: Current American Heart Association nutrition guidance recommends comparing Nutrition Facts labels and choosing products with less sodium; it also recommends using herbs, spices, citrus, and other flavorings in place of added salt. AHA notes that most dietary sodium comes from packaged, prepared, and restaurant foods, so taste alone or removing only the saltshaker is not sufficient. Therefore, A demonstrates correct understanding. B and C underestimate hidden sodium, and D reverses the advised dietary strategy.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Directly supports label reading, lower-sodium food selection, limiting sodium from packaged/prepared foods, and using herbs/spices/citrus/vinegar instead of salt without imposing a heart-failure-specific universal sodium target.
candidate.source_document_title: How to Reduce Sodium in Your Diet; AHA Diet and Lifestyle Recommendations
candidate.source_locator: How to Reduce Sodium in Your Diet → shopping: compare packaged/prepared-food labels and select lower-sodium products; preparation: use onions, garlic, herbs, spices, citrus juices, and vinegars instead of salt. AHA Diet and Lifestyle Recommendations → choose whole/minimally processed foods, foods low in sodium/prepared with little or no salt, and read Nutrition Facts/ingredient labels. Sodium Sources guidance: more than 70% of U.S. dietary sodium comes from packaged or restaurant foods.
candidate.source_version_date: AHA Diet and Lifestyle Recommendations last reviewed 2026-03-31; sodium guidance current 2026
candidate.stem: A client with heart failure has been advised to reduce dietary sodium. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding of practical sodium-reduction strategies?
